subject: Selecting the access corridor for Redwood Private: direct peering, endpoint-only, or encrypted tunnel
messages:
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Sam Hollis <sam.hollis@enneahealth.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 31 Aug 2026 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: Selecting the access corridor for Redwood Private: direct peering, endpoint-only, or encrypted tunnel

Hi Sam —

Thanks again for the demo last week. Per our conversation, I put together the three connectivity patterns that Ennea uses most often with Redwood Private and a short table of tradeoffs so your engineering and security teams can weigh the right factors for your pilot. I attached a concise PDF ("ennea-network-options-v2.pdf") that includes the sketch and an estimated timeline for a PoC.

Quick summary up front:
- VPC peering (cross-account peering) — best latency, simplest packet path; requires route/ARP management and careful route table planning across accounts. Not ideal if Ennea needs strict tenant isolation or limited route exposure.
- Interface endpoints / PrivateLink — preferred when you want granular access control and minimal surface area. Operates over the cloud provider's private endpoint plane; reduces blast radius but can add egress NAT considerations for service-initiated callbacks.
- Site-to-site IPsec VPN — fastest to stand up for PoCs, works for on-prem datacenters and transit networks. Bandwidth, MTU, and long-term operational cost (reliability/monitoring) are the tradeoffs.

Factors you mentioned to prioritize: compliance (data plane isolation), low tail latency for synchronous inference, and working within Ennea's cross-account networking policies. If useful, Kimberly can run a short perf simulation (baseline token latency delta) across the three modes with a small load shape representative of your production traffic.

Proposed next steps:
1) Ennea to confirm compliance constraints (allowed cross-account peering? mandated endpoint-only?)
2) Redwood + Ennea schedule a 60-min technical sync (I can invite Kimberly and Marissa)
3) Choose PoC path (we typically do PrivateLink + a warm S2S VPN as fallback for regulated customers)
Attaching: ennea-network-options-v2.pdf (overview) and a blank MA plan spreadsheet you can edit.

Thanks — talk soon.

— Stephanie Nguyen
Business Development Manager | Redwood Inference
stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com

Thanks Stephanie — this is helpful. A couple quick clarifications from my side:

- Ennea's security policy prefers to avoid broad peering where possible; that said, we do allow project-to-project peering if routes are scoped and require an approved exception.
- Our on-call SRE team is concerned about callback traffic from inference servers back to customer-managed services (e.g., artifact fetch, audit webhooks). How does PrivateLink vs peering affect outbound flows?

Also, can you share any operational runbook items (SLA incident playbook / monitoring hooks) that differ by connectivity mode? We want to assess operational burden.

Sam

From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>
To: Sam Hollis <sam.hollis@enneahealth.com>
Cc: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>

Subject: Re: Selecting the access corridor for Redwood Private: direct peering, endpoint-only, or encrypted tunnel

On Mon, 31 Aug 2026 at 10:08, Sam Hollis <sam.hollis@enneahealth.com> wrote:
> Thanks Stephanie — this is helpful. A couple quick clarifications from my side:
>
> - Ennea's security policy prefers to avoid broad peering where possible; that said, we do allow project-to-project peering if routes are scoped and require an approved exception.
> - Our on-call SRE team is concerned about callback traffic from inference servers back to customer-managed services (e.g., artifact fetch, audit webhooks). How does PrivateLink vs peering affect outbound flows?
>
> Also, can you share any operational runbook items (SLA incident playbook / monitoring hooks) that differ by connectivity mode? We want to assess operational burden.
>
Hi Sam — thanks for the questions. Looping in Kimberly (network solutions) and Marissa (deployment engineering) to give concrete tradeoffs and a short operational checklist. Below are quick answers; Kimberly and Marissa will add specifics in the sync.

Outbound / callback flows:
- VPC peering: Ennea IPs can reach Redwood instances directly; callbacks originate from Redwood's compute private IPs back to Ennea services via peering. That means you must add route entries in your side and consider NAT if you want egress to appear from a stable IP range. Avoids internet egress but requires route controls.
- PrivateLink (interface endpoint): Callbacks typically traverse the customer's network via the endpoint's elastic network interfaces. For some cloud providers, service-side outbound flows may be SNAT'd to the endpoint owner depending on the implementation; this can necessitate a small egress IP mapping table or a NAT gateway on your side for predictable source IPs.
- S2S VPN: Callbacks use the tunnel; NAT behavior depends on your gateway implementation. VPN is straightforward when you require on-prem termination, but you need to account for throughput ceilings and MTU (we've seen packaged inference shards suffer ~2-4% throughput drop if PMTU isn't adjusted).

Operational runbook differences (short):
- Peering: route table validation + BGP / routing policy doc; monitoring: VPC flow logs + active ping checks to a pinned probe address; failover: pre-configured alternate peered route or PrivateLink fallback.
- PrivateLink: endpoint health checks + more granular IAM/policy review; monitoring: endpoint connection metrics + interface ENI health; failover: can route traffic to hosted fallback (public-hosted API with mTLS).
- VPN: monitor tunnel uptime and retransmit stats; NOC playbook to trigger failover to PrivateLink or alternate VPN path. Include monthly rekey and churn windows.

Recommendation for Ennea pilot given your constraints:
If Ennea cannot accept broad peering, my recommendation is to start with PrivateLink for the pilot (minimal surface area, satisfies least-privilege requirements), and run a parallel temporary S2S VPN for broader traffic flows and as a fallback. That combination gives predictable access control while allowing us to validate latency SLOs.

Kimberly & Marissa — could you commit to a quick perf run (30–60 minutes) and a one-page ops checklist we can share with Sam before the sync?

Thanks,
— Stephanie

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Sam Hollis <sam.hollis@enneahealth.com>
Cc: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 31 Aug 2026 16:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Selecting the access corridor for Redwood Private: direct peering, endpoint-only, or encrypted tunnel

Hi Sam —

Quick follow-up from our engineering side after a short internal sweep. Key nuggets for your SREs to consider before the sync: 

1) MTU and path MTU discovery: if you use S2S VPN and your on-prem appliance defaults to a low MTU, you'll want to tune fragmentation for large payload transfers (model artifact pulls). We recommend enabling PMTU probing and testing with 3x payload sizes.

2) Token-level latency: PrivateLink adds ~3–8 ms on average vs peering in the same region for short-sequence inference (our internal median). For most synchronous features this is acceptable and trades off for improved isolation.

3) Egress IPs for webhook/callbacks: we can provide a small set of stable egress IPs for PrivateLink flows via our managed NAT pool if Ennea needs allowlisting. We documented the process in the attached PDF.

4) Monitoring hooks: we will push a CloudWatch/Stackdriver exporter for endpoint metrics and a short Grafana dashboard template. Incident playbook: connectivity degraded -> validate ENI health / route table / tunnel -> fail traffic to hosted fallback (with rate limiting).

If that aligns, I'll create the one-page ops checklist and a short perf script (kubernetes job + small load generator) and drop both into the Drive folder. Ready to sync tomorrow or Wednesday afternoon — what works for you?

— Marissa
Deployment Engineering | Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.com
